# Stress tests: bounds on the principle {#sec-stress}

The principle could be an artifact of the settings in which we found it. When every
layer can read every earlier position, carrying is never necessary. When the content
is visible in the text, it can always be re-read. We therefore test three settings
chosen to make carrying useful or invisible: an architecture in which most layers can
pass information forward only by carrying it, a distance at which most attention
layers cannot reach the source, and content that is not in the text at all. Each test
has a decision rule committed before its first result (Appendix @sec-app-prereg). The
tests bound the principle: they measure which route the model uses when carrying is
available, and how far that choice moves when lookup becomes harder. @fig-stress
summarizes them.

![Stress tests. **A:** Qwen3.5 hybrids, in which three of every four layers are
recurrent. With the donor state allowed to enter only one layer type at the source,
the plan reaches the rhyme through the attention layers (blue). Entry through the recurrent layers,
which can only relay (purple), produces 2 to 4% of persistence, below the committed

line 1 and line 2, at the measured distances only. Past the 1,024-token window of its
local layers (shaded), direct retrieval of the rhyme word falls, the stored copy at
the line's final token becomes necessary for about half of persistence, and early
relay rises to 12%, between the committed stop and go lines. Side panels: absolute
persistence, and the share of second lines that still rhyme in four models. **C:**
hidden choice, as shares of the text-swap reference: not reproduced by the post-list

## Recurrent memory {#sec-recurrent}

Qwen3.5 [@qwen2026qwen35] interleaves three Gated DeltaNet layers
[@yang2025gateddeltanet] with each full-attention layer. A recurrent layer holds a
fixed-size state that is updated position by position. In those layers, information
from the source can reach a later position only by being carried in that state: relay
by construction, and invisible in the text. The attention layers can still retrieve.
The test therefore asks which route the model uses when both are available. We split
persistence by layer type. In the *attention-only* cell, the donor state enters at the
source, but the input of every recurrent layer at the source is restored to its clean
value, so the edit can move forward only through the attention layers. The
*recurrent-only* cell is the converse. A cell with both routes blocked is a sanity
check. The rule committed in advance was "go" if recurrent-only is at least 25% of
persistence with its interval above zero, and "stop" if it is below 10%. It is decided
on the largest model; smaller sizes give the trend.

When both routes are open, the donor signal travels through the attention layers. At 4B and 9B (40 couplets each), the
recurrent-only cell is \(+0.28\) [0.07, 0.49] and \(+0.55\) [0.31, 0.79]: 3% and 4% of
persistence. The attention-only cell accounts for 97% and 96%. At the decisive size,
27B (48 recurrent and 16 attention layers; 24 couplets), recurrent-only is \(+0.41\)
[0.18, 0.64], 2% of persistence \(+18.8\) [16.3, 21.3], and attention-only 95%. The
both-blocked cell is exactly zero in every model. Decision: stop. Although three
quarters of the layers can pass the plan forward only by carrying it, the plan travels
by direct retrieval through the quarter that can look it up. The design controls
which layer type receives the donor signal at the source; it does not isolate every
later path through each layer type, so it measures the share of donor entry, not the
recurrent memory's natural share. Entry through the recurrent layers is small but
nonzero, which bounds the principle at 2 to 4% of persistence for this architecture.

## Beyond the attention window {#sec-distance}

Gemma 3 alternates five local layers with a 1,024-token sliding window with one
global layer [@gemma3; @beltagy2020longformer]. Once line 1 lies more than 1,024
tokens before the rhyme position, five of six layers can no longer read it. We
insert \(D\) tokens of neutral filler, a seeded arrangement of fixed everyday
sentences, at the start of the model's turn, followed by a fixed cue (`Next line:`).
The model then writes line 2. Relay is split into three groups: the stored copy (the
prompt positions after line 1), the filler, and the generated text (the cue and
line 2). The committed decision number is the share of persistence relayed through
the generated text: "go" at 25% or more, "stop" below 10%, and extension to 50
couplets in between. A full-attention control, Qwen3-14B, showed before the Gemma
result that relay *shares* can rise with distance only because direct retrieval
weakens. We therefore added, before that result, the rule that a rise counts only if
absolute relay also grows.

@tbl-distance gives the extended run. At 2,000 tokens, Gemma 3 27B still writes a
rhyming line 2 in 82% of couplets, but persistence falls from \(+42.4\) to \(+26.4\).
The model reads less of the plan from the rhyme word: direct retrieval falls from 66%
to 40% of persistence. It relies instead on the stored copy at the line's final token,
which is necessary for \(+13.0\) [10.0, 16.1], about half of persistence. Absolute
relay grows about thirteenfold (\(+1.0\) to \(+13.1\)), mostly through the stored copy.
The filler relays nothing (\(+0.3\) by sufficiency, \(+0.15\) by necessity). Relay
along the generated text rises from about 1% to 12% by sufficiency (\(+3.2\) [2.2,
4.3]); its necessity is \(+2.7\), or 10%. This block contains the cue and all of line 2,
including its last three positions, so it mixes early relay with the late lookup; the
split was not run. It is the largest relay through generated text in any setting and
the one clear exception to the principle. By the committed rule it falls between
"stop" and "go", and it remains inconclusive: even at 2,000 tokens it is a minority
route, about an eighth of the effect.

The window curve, committed before its result, predicted a change specifically
between 1,000 and 1,500 tokens (18 couplets per distance). It is only partly
supported. Direct retrieval is 66%, 64%, 54%, 40% and 40% of persistence at 0, 500,
1,000, 1,500 and 2,000 tokens, and the stored copy is necessary for 11%, 25%, 30%,
45% and 49%. The steepest step is where line 1 leaves the window, but the shift has
begun at 500 tokens, inside it. Relay through the generated text is 11%, 9%, 13% and
12% at the four nonzero distances: it appears once filler is present and does not
grow with distance. We therefore describe a long-distance shift toward the stored
copy, steepest across the window, rather than a window-edge mechanism.

stored copy: sufficiency / necessity & $+0.1$ / $+4.6$ (11\%) & $+9.7$ / \textbf{$+13.0$} (49\%)\\

Relay at a distance, Gemma 3 27B (chat prompt; 50 couplets per distance; 95%
intervals). Shares are of persistence at the same distance. At \(D=0\) the generated
text's necessity is the late lookup.

:::

Three further models show what happens when lookup gets harder without a strong stored
copy. They also separate distance from the window.

- *Gemma 3 12B*, which stores little at the line end (@tbl-storage), loses the plan.
  The window curve, committed before its result, predicted that the plan would
  survive while line 1 is inside the window (500 and 1,000 tokens) and vanish outside
  it. Instead, the plan fades gradually and is mostly gone inside the window.
  Second lines rhyme in 100%, 39%, 8%, 0% and 0% of couplets at 0, 500, 1,000, 1,500
  and 2,000 tokens, and persistence falls from \(+40.5\) to \(+11.5\) [8.1, 14.9] at 500
  tokens and \(+4.0\) at 1,000. At 12B the loss reflects the distance itself, not the
  window. Relay never takes over: absolute relay stays at \(+0.8\) to \(+2.3\), and
  early relay at or below \(+0.9\).
- *Qwen3.5-9B*, a hybrid whose attention layers have no window, also fades: rhyming
  falls from 92% to 4% at 2,000 tokens. What remains of persistence (\(+3.6\)) is still
  81% direct retrieval, and absolute relay does not grow (\(+1.2\) to \(+0.8\)).
- *Qwen3-14B*, with full attention, largely abandons the task after the filler (8%
  rhyming), and its absolute relay stays flat (\(+2.3\) to \(+2.8\)).

Across the four models, distance moves reliance onto a stored copy where one exists,
and otherwise costs the plan. No model responds by carrying the plan along the text it
writes, beyond the 12% in Gemma 3 27B. The rhyme word and the line's final token lie at
the same distance from the target, yet the global layers of Gemma 3 27B read the
line-end token. This fits the view of separator tokens as long-range summaries of
their segment [@chen2024sepllm; @wang2023labelwords; @xiao2024sinks].

## Hidden content {#sec-hidden}

In every task so far, the content is visible: a reader of the text could recover the
rhyme sound from line 1, or the value from the operands. The case monitoring cares
about is content that cannot be recovered from the text. We create it with a secret
choice. The prompt reads: "Secretly choose one fruit from this list: {4 fruits}. Do not
write your choice yet. First write one sentence about the weather. Then write the
fruit you chose." Under greedy decoding the pick is a deterministic function of the
prompt. It depends on the model's own preferences and on the list order, so no reader
can compute it. For the route split, the model's turn is prefilled with a fixed
weather sentence and "The fruit I chose is". The outcome is the log-odds of the
donor's pick against the original pick at the next token.

**Mostly re-derived, partly stored, barely relayed.** The donor is the same list in
another order, chosen so that the greedy pick differs. The reference is a *text swap*:
the donor order written into the prompt, which moves the pick by construction. In
Qwen3-8B, Gemma 3 12B and Gemma 3 27B (100 pairs each), donor states at the prompt
positions after the list move the reveal by 12%, 15% and 16% of the text swap. The
reveal reads all of it directly: the retrieval cell equals the post-list effect. Relay
of this stored part through the sentence is \(+0.00\) [\(-0.04\), 0.05], \(-0.06\)
[\(-0.14\), 0.01] and \(-0.01\) [\(-0.10\), 0.08]; it is also zero within its interval in
Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-14B. The rest of the pick, 84 to 88%, is re-derived at the reveal
from the visible list. The two largest Qwen models are the exception.

- In *Qwen3-32B*, relay through the sentence is small but nonzero: \(+0.06\) [0.04,
  0.09]. That is 2% of the text swap but one eighth of the stored part.
- In the recurrent hybrid *Qwen3.5-27B*, relay of the stored part is \(+0.03\) [0.02,
  0.04]: 1% of the text swap and one sixth of the stored part. Its sentence positions
  themselves account for 7% of the text swap (\(+0.15\) [0.12, 0.18]); Qwen3.5-9B gives the
same pattern (relay 2%, sentence positions 8%). These are the largest in any model; Qwen3-4B has 5% and every other model at most 1%. This is
  expected when every position's recurrent state summarizes the prefix, including the
  list.

**What is stored.** An order swap cannot separate a stored pick from a stored copy of
the list order. In the out-of-list control, the donor list shares no item with the
original, so the donor's pick does not occur in the prompt at all. The committed
criterion is that post-list donor states raise the absent pick, and it holds in every
model. After the first results we identified a confound: the positions might hold a
copy of the donor's list rather than its pick. We therefore added, post hoc, *pick
specificity*: the effect on the donor's pick minus the mean effect on the donor's other
items. We then committed it, before the results, as the primary measure of a
replication in a second domain (animals; disjoint lists of six). The replication
confirms that pick-specific information is stored after the list, in both families
(@fig-stress C; @tbl-hidden). A same-pick null, committed before its result, gives the
converse check. The donor is the same list in another order with the *same* pick.
Post-list donor states then leave the relative preference for the pick unchanged on
average in Gemma 3 12B: \(-0.19\) [\(-0.53\), 0.16], against \(+1.01\) [0.78, 1.24] with
out-of-list donors. \pending{same-pick null at Gemma 3 27B.}

These controls do not settle what the stored information is. The post-list positions
could hold the pick itself. They could also hold a copy of the list from which the
reveal re-derives the pick by applying the model's preference. Both accounts predict
pick specificity with out-of-list donors, and both predict the same-pick null. We
therefore claim only that information specific to the pick, and absent from the
visible text, is stored after the list and read at the reveal.

The families diverge with scale.

- In Gemma the stored share grows with generation and size. Gemma 3 stores 18 to 22%
  at 4B, 15 to 18% at 12B and 31 to 40% at 27B. The committed monotone prediction (4B
  below 12B below 27B) is only partly supported, because 4B stores more than 12B.
  Gemma 4 31B stores 82% (fruits; \(+2.93\) [2.56, 3.30]) and 91% (animals; \(+4.44\)
  [3.97, 4.93]) of the text swap's pick specificity. For Gemma 4 the route split was
  not run.
- In Qwen3 the stored share shrinks with scale: 10 to 15% at 8B, 0 to 7% at 14B and 32B.
  Qwen3.5-27B stores 3 to 4%. Larger Qwen models re-derive the pick at the reveal.

Stored pick-specific information: pick specificity of the post-list edit as a share of
the text-swap pick specificity (100 pairs per cell; values with 95% intervals in
Appendix @sec-app-hidden). Fruits: specificity added post hoc. Animals: committed before
the result.

:::

**Not written into the text.** In the free version, the model writes its own weather
sentence. The sentence changes with the donor in 17 to 45% of pairs, but it never names
an item. Emission is \(+0.02\) [\(-0.03\), 0.08], \(-0.01\) [\(-0.07\), 0.04] and \(-0.00\)
in Qwen3-8B, Gemma 3 12B and Gemma 3 27B. The written sentence has no measurable causal
effect on the reveal.

**Where it is stored.** Per-token necessity over the post-list block localizes the
stored information (@fig-sites B).

- In Gemma 3 27B, 77% of the pick-specific effect (\(+1.91\) [1.57, 2.24] of \(+2.48\))
  sits on a single token: *the* in "about the weather". The period after the list
  accounts for \(+0.42\), and the period ending the instruction \(+0.22\). Every other
  token, including the end-of-turn and role tokens, is \(0.00\pm0.05\).
- Gemma 3 12B uses the same site with fruits (*the*: \(+0.52\) of \(+1.03\); the period
  after the list: \(+0.32\)) and with animals (*the*: \(+1.04\) [0.80, 1.28] of
  \(+1.42\), 73%).
- Gemma 3 4B stores as much (18 to 22%) but places it mostly on the periods that close
  the list and the instruction (91% with fruits, 65% with animals), with a function word
  taking the rest (7% on *the* with fruits; 32% on *your* with animals).

The decisive check, committed before its result, changes the wording. If the storage
moves with the function words, it is storage at a predictable low-content token. If it
stays at a fixed position or spreads out, the site is template-specific. We reworded
the instruction to "Keep your choice private for now. Begin by describing today's
weather in a single sentence. After that, reveal which fruit you picked." Gemma 3 12B
then stores 12% of the text swap's pick specificity (\(+0.59\) [0.38, 0.81]), again on
two low-content tokens. The period that ends the list accounts for \(+0.42\) [0.21,
0.63] (71%), and the apostrophe of "today's", the token before "weather", for \(+0.16\)
[0.09, 0.22] (27%). Every other token is below 0.04. Gemma 3 4B moves the same way: the
apostrophe of "today's" takes 69% (\(+0.54\) [0.46, 0.62]) and the list-closing period
28%. At both sizes, the function-word site moved with the wording.
\pending{reworded instruction at Gemma 3 27B.}

Across sizes and wordings, the stored information sits on two or three low-content
tokens. These are the punctuation that closes a segment (the list or the instruction)
and one function word of the instruction, whose identity depends on the wording ("the",
"your", or the possessive before "weather"). Segment-closing punctuation is
the analogue of the line's final token for rhymes. In both tasks the model stores a
copy once, at a boundary next to the source or at a predictable token of the prompt,
and reads it at the point of use.
